extracted.intended_audience: criminalists, forensic investigators, judges and legal examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on observing and interpreting nonverbal signs, voice, color changes, and biographical clues to assess character, veracity, and motive in suspects and witnesses. Emphasizes cautious corroboration, timing, and using multiple indices rather than single cues as proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestures as indicators of inner state (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definite bodily expressions (gestures) are often transmitted and modified culturally and can indicate inner mental states but identical inner states do not invariably have identical bodily concomitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gestures as informative signs but be cautious: physiological, anatomical, atavistic influences, personal habits, inheritance, and individual variation make generalization hazardous. Treat gestures as approximate, hypothetical indicators, not definitive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradiction between words and gestures signals deception
rubrics_metrics.description: When speech and gesture contradict (e.g., saying 'she went down' while pointing up), the gesture may be the truer expression and indicate the speaker's unconscious truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for mismatches between verbal content and simultaneous gestures; such contradictions can reveal deception because gestures are often unwatched and automatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specific gestures as corroborative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct, significant gestures can corroborate or reveal details of a narrated act (e.g., pressing fingers to thigh when describing smothering suggests actual action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clearly meaningful, spontaneous gesture accompanying a testimony can justify questioning or follow-up; treat such gestures as strong leads to probe further rather than as standalone proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of overvaluing gestures when observation is imperfect
rubrics_metrics.description: The certainty of inference from gestures is endangered if observations are difficult: observers may mistake habitual or indifferent gestures for significant ones or make their observations too noticeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on gestures when you lack clear observation skill; do not advertise that you're watching (witness will control gestures). Prefer repeated, calm observation and begin with simple cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin studies with simple, everyday cases
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not begin observational study with murder and robbery but with simple daily-life cases where mistakes are less likely and observation can be calm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train on commonplace phenomena to build skill before tackling complex criminal cases; use plentiful ordinary examples to learn reliable indices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity of sensation produces bodily expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Any sensation that exceeds a certain intensity usually expresses itself in bodily activity (Herbert Spencer); more intense feelings more readily cause observable gestures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that strong emotions (anger, fear, pain) will produce bodily signs; lighter, superficial sensations may not produce clear expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and acquired crystallization of gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Through generations and training, certain bodily expressions become fixed types (face and hands especially) and can be recognized as characteristic of social roles or professions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use knowledge of culturally transmitted expression-types (e.g., occupational posture, cultivated gestures) as part of characterization, but beware overhasty typological conclusions (see Lombroso critique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice timbre as an emotional indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: The timbre (tone) of speech correlates with emotional states: high tone with mild complaint, deep groans or piercing shrieks with extreme pain, questioning tones when unsure, hoarseness in the wounded, a characteristic 'cold and toneless' voice in denying criminals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use voice quality as corroborative evidence of state; note physiological concomitants (mouth snapping, swallowing, carotid palpitation). Do not rely on voice alone — timbres are under-studied and can deceive; simulation is difficult to sustain but possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological signs accompanying voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiological changes (e.g., palpitation visible at the right carotid) accompany certain vocal timbres and can be diagnostic of nervous stimulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe accompanying physical signs when judging voice; combined physiological and vocal observations strengthen inference but are not conclusive by themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborative value of vocal and gestural signs (not sole proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment based on voice or gesture has great corroborative value but is insufficient as an independent means of proof because timbres may deceive and observations are imperfectly studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat vocal/gestural observations as supportive evidence to be corroborated by other facts; avoid treating them as definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative accompaniment and social contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers/spectators tend to involuntarily imitate actions they see (e.g., moving along with fencers or keeping step with a marcher); many daily phenomena (nodding, shrugging) are spontaneous accompaniments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the environment can induce mimicry; distinguish between spontaneous gestures indicative of inner state and automatic imitation triggered by witnessing similar actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal influence of expression and emotion (‘talking-yourself-into-it’)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixing an expression or adopting an attitude can produce the corresponding emotion in oneself (imitating angry look → actually becoming angry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that a convincingly presented emotion may be self-induced by posture/gesture rather than a spontaneous inner state; this explains how suspects can 'work themselves into' apparent passion without deceitful mummery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing and reading can produce emotional changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing or reading has the same alarming influence on voice and general appearance as speaking and acting; written presentation can evoke or reinforce emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider written statements as capable of producing genuine emotional expressions; do not assume written calm equates to inner calm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of observation: early versus late presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Early in a fabricated narrative gestures are often awkward and exaggerated; later, once a subject becomes lost in the presentation, gestures become natural and mimic genuine excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe witnesses early in their account to detect forced, exaggerated gestures; check whether word and gesture soon conform — rapid conformity after theatrical exaggeration suggests the subject has elicited the emotion themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruity between word and gesture as a test
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether there is consistent congruity between speech and gesture; habitual lack of congruity may be honest for some people, but swift alignment after lively presentation suggests self-induced or skilful feigning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use congruity patterns as part of credibility assessment; account for individual variability (theatrical people gesticulate more).

rubrics_metrics.name: Color changes: pallor (paling) assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Paleness results from venous muscle cramp and can be artificially produced by chest contraction and glottis closure, but this trick is obvious and of little practical use; pallor occurs only in intense excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paleness is rare and tied to strong emotion (anger, fear, pain); it is of limited evidential value and can be misleading (fear of unmasking vs guilt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Color changes: blushing assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Blushing is a transitory vascular reaction, sometimes mechanically producible, common across cultures, more frequent in youth and women; blushing by itself offers no reliable evidence of guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer guilt from blushing alone—many people blush without culpability; note that blushing can cause confusion and impair testimony. Mechanical or auxiliary blushing (rubbing, chemicals) exists but is rarely useful in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make capital of statements made during blush
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the blush itself causes confusion, statements made while someone is blushing are unreliable and should not be exploited as evidence of guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a witness or accused is visibly blushing, avoid pressing or treating their utterances from that moment as conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble many small indices of character (general signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small habitual signs (how a man wears his hat, shoes, umbrella use, eating habits, cleanliness) can be highly instructive about character when many such observations are aggregated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mundane, repetitive observations as indices that suggest hypotheses about character; they must be corroborative and only suggest 'perhaps the case is the same to-day' rather than serving as proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain a general view of a person’s life and earlier conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand a deed you must relate it to the total character and life-course of the doer; learning about a suspect's earlier life, wishes, beliefs and pleasures is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interview suspects and important witnesses not just about the immediate deed but about life history, needs, pleasures, and worldview; these inform predispositions and motives and make understanding of acts possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use people's judgments of others as projective indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: A person’s praise or condemnation of others typically reflects what he does or avoids himself; thus judgments about others reveal the speaker’s own character and preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how subjects judge others to infer their own tendencies and needs; this is a low-effort but revealing technique when used carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider opportunity and needs as revealing of motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Opportunity (occasions) and a person’s needs/pleasures expose what a person is and indicate what might drive them to commit acts; 'Occasiones hominem fragilem non faciunt, sed, qualis sit, ostendunt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether opportunity and specific needs were present; discovering a real need behind a deed explains the power used to commit it and helps relate crime to character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of sweeping, undemonstrated theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid building far-reaching theoretical claims (e.g., Lombroso’s criminal stigmata) on inadequate, unstudied material; do not assert without consideration that far-reaching statements are justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor careful observation, richer material, and better instruments over bold generalizations; remain skeptical of grand typologies unless robustly supported.
